title: Importunate questions demand demonstration of the indemonstrable
source_text: XXVI. Quod autem spectat importunas illas interrogationes, Unde probatis Apostolos fuisse & scripsisse libros instinctu divino, & eos qui circumferuntur revera illorum esse? Resp. a nobis aliquid injustum exigi, nempe ut demonstremus quod est indemonstrabile. Itaque fatemur ultro ista non posse a nobis demonstrari, & mathematice seu logice probari. Sed inde negamus sequi libros istos esse non posse certam & primam fidei regulam; quoniam hoc proprium est principiis fidei ut sint inevidentia, neque probari possint argumentis philosophice necessariis & evidentibus. Quae tamen ita accipienda non sunt, ut jam saepe observatum est, quasi nihil habeamus quod hominibus profanis regerere possimus, & impiis eorum quaestionibus opponere. Nobis enim non desunt argumenta quae viro prudenti satis esse possint, & ipsi suadere Apostolos & Prophetas instinctu divino scripsisse, & nos in manibus habere genuinos eorum libros: cujus generis argumenta multa harum thesium parte prima, proposuimus & explicuimus, nec opus est hic illa repetere. Hoc solum fatemur argumenta illa non habere evidentiam logicam, seu mathematicam, & eatenus rem relinquere incertam, si libet incertum vocare quod est inevidens, & ἀναπόδεικτον. Sed hoc quoque addimus, si quid incertitudinis argumenta illa relinquunt, minime tolli posse per Ecclesiae quoddam judicium & determinationem, ut jamjam probatum est.
pass_a_gloss: But as for those importunate interrogations, Whence do you prove that the Apostles were and wrote books by divine instinct, and that those which circulate are truly theirs? Reply: something unjust is demanded of us, namely that we demonstrate what is indemonstrable. Therefore we freely confess that those things cannot be demonstrated by us and proved mathematically or logically. But thence we deny that it follows that those books cannot be a certain and first rule of faith; because it is proper to the principles of faith that they be non-evident, and cannot be proved by arguments philosophically necessary and evident. Which things nevertheless are not to be so taken, as has often been observed, as if we had nothing that we could retort to profane people and oppose to their impious questions. For we do not lack arguments that can be enough for a prudent man, and persuade him that the Apostles and Prophets wrote by divine instinct, and that we have their genuine books in our hands: of which kind of arguments we proposed and explained many in the first part of these theses, and there is no need to repeat them here. This alone we confess, that those arguments do not have logical or mathematical evidence, and to that extent leave the matter uncertain, if one likes to call uncertain what is non-evident and undemonstrable (Greek anapodeikton). But this too we add: if those arguments leave any uncertainty, it can by no means be removed by some judgment and determination of the Church, as has just been proved.
pass_b_english: As for those importunate questions — How do you prove the Apostles existed and wrote by divine impulse, and that the circulating books are truly theirs? — something unjust is being demanded of us: that we demonstrate what is indemonstrable.

We freely admit that we cannot demonstrate those things mathematically or logically. We deny that it follows that those books cannot be faith's certain first rule. It belongs to faith's principles to be non-evident and not provable by philosophically necessary and evident arguments.

That does not mean we have nothing to answer profane objectors. We have arguments enough for a prudent person — that the Apostles and Prophets wrote by divine impulse, and that we hold their genuine books — many of which we already set out in Part I of these theses; there is no need to repeat them here.

We only grant that those arguments lack logical or mathematical evidence, and so leave the matter "uncertain" if one chooses to call the non-evident and undemonstrable (anapodeikton) uncertain. Even so, whatever uncertainty they leave cannot be cleared by some church judgment or determination — as we have just proved.

choices.why: Greek for what lacks demonstrative proof.
